subject: Computer Networking
title: TCP: Reliable Delivery
description: Learn TCP: Reliable Delivery in one minute.

hook.text: You download a file. Every byte arrives perfectly. That reliability doesn't happen by accident.

buildup.text: TCP numbers every packet and tracks which ones arrived. If one is missing, it requests a resend.

discovery.text: Before sending data, TCP does a handshake — both sides agree they're ready. Then transfer begins.

twist.text: All that checking adds overhead. TCP is reliable but slower than alternatives like UDP.

climax.text: Web browsing, email, file transfers — anything that needs accuracy uses TCP under the hood.

punchline.text: TCP guarantees every packet arrives. No exceptions.

quiz.question: What does TCP do if a packet is lost during transmission?
options: Requests the missing packet to be resent
Restarts the entire transfer from scratch

details.summary: TCP ensures data arrives complete and in order by numbering packets, requiring acknowledgments, and retransmitting lost packets. It provides reliable delivery at the cost of some speed. TCP is used for web pages, email, file transfers, and any application that cannot tolerate missing data.
details.whyItMatters: TCP's reliability makes the web, email, and file transfer work correctly. Without it, missing packets would produce corrupted pages and incomplete downloads.
takeaways: TCP numbers packets and requires acknowledgment of receipt
TCP sacrifices speed for guaranteed complete delivery

faq.question: How does TCP detect lost packets?
faq.answer: TCP uses acknowledgment timers. When the sender does not receive an acknowledgment within the expected time, it assumes the packet was lost and retransmits. The receiver can also signal gaps using selective acknowledgment, telling the sender exactly which packets are missing.

faq.question: Why does TCP slow down during congestion?
faq.answer: TCP uses congestion control algorithms that reduce sending speed when packet loss is detected. Loss usually indicates network congestion. By slowing down, TCP prevents overwhelming the network. All TCP connections cooperatively reduce their rates during congestion.
